DO NOT DISTRIBUTE. <!-- image --> ## Conflict of Interest Statement The presenters do not have a financial interest, arrangement or affiliation with any organization that could be perceived as a real or apparent conflict of interest in the context of this presentation. <!-- image --> 2 ## Learning Objectives - 1.Describe the pharmacology of insulin preparations with respect to onset and duration of action, listing the primary preparation(s) in each group. - 2.Describe the mechanisms of action, use, and adverse effects of hypoglycemic agents for the treatment of diabetes mellitus: sulfonylureas, biguanides, thiazolidinediones, alpha-glucosidase inhibitors, GLP-1 agonists, amylin agonist, DPP-4 inhibitors, SGLT2 inhibitors, glinides. - 3.Describe underlying co-morbidities that impact the choice of hypoglycemic agents. <!-- image --> ## Diagnosis of Diabetes (ADA) A hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) level of 6.5% or higher; or A fasting plasma glucose (FPG) level of 126 mg/dL (7 mmol/L) or higher; fasting is defined as no caloric intake for at least 8 hours, or A 2-hour plasma glucose level of 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or higher during a 75-g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), or A random plasma glucose of 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or higher in a patient with classic symptoms of hyperglycemia (i.e., polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, weight loss) or hyperglycemic crisis <!-- image --> ## Diabetes Mellitus Chronic disease characterized by hyperglycemia and glucosuria. ## Type 1 (T1D) Patient secretes little to no insulin (absolute deficiency). Insulin resistance and relative insulin deficiency. Associated with obesity, dyslipidemia, hypertension, and other conditions. <!-- image --> <!-- image --> Source: Lippincott's Illustrated Review of Pharmacology, 7 th Ed. ## DM Characteristics | Onset | Type 1 Most often abrupt | Type 2 Gradual | |---------------------------------|----------------------------------|----------------------------------------------| | Clinical Symptoms | Polydipsia, polyphagia, polyuria | Often none | | Ketosis | Frequent | Infrequent (except with infection or stress) | | Endogenous Insulin | Negligible | Present but often ineffective | | Insulin Therapy | Immediate | Years after diagnosis | | Non-Insulin Hypoglycemic Agents | Rarely used | Clinically indicated | <!-- image --> ## Drug-Induced Causes of Type 2 Diabetes Glucocorticoids Thyroid hormones β-blockers Post-transplant drugs - (tacrolimus, cyclosporine, sirolimus) Thiazides Anti-retrovirals Anti-psychotics Statins <!-- image --> Nicotinic acid <!-- image --> ## Case A 19 yo woman with Type 1 DM on insulin presents to your clinic for routine follow up. She was diagnosed with Type 1 DM 3 months ago, and she is currently taking insulin glargine 32 units at nighttime, and insulin aspart 6 units with breakfast, 6 units with lunch and 8 units with dinner. She denies any sweats, confusion, jitteriness. She brings her meter with her today, which shows fasting AM blood sugars of 170-190, with post-prandial sugars of 120-150. Increased secretion of insulin from the pancreas <!-- image --> Group 3 - Drugs that Lower Glucose Levels by Actions on Liver, Muscle, Adipose tissue, and Brain ## Thiazolidinediones ('Glitazones' or TZDs) Agent: pioglitazone ## MOA: - PPAR-Υ activators (peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma) in adipocytes - Peripheral 'Insulin sensitizer': promotes fatty acid uptake peripherally - Increase muscle, fat and liver sensitivity to insulin by decreasing free fatty acids levels Effect on Weight: Increased ("but it's good fat") HbA1c: up to 0.5-1.4% reduction Side effects: risk of hypoglycemia, weight gain, fluid retention, hepatotoxicity <!-- image --> ## Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) Receptor Agonists and GIP/GLP-1 Dual Agonists* ## MOA - Potentiates glucose-stimulated insulin secretion - Depresses glucagon secretion - Delays gastric emptying - Suppresses appetite HbA1c: up to lowered by 1.5% Effect on Weight: Decrease (3-4kg)* *Weight loss greater with semaglutide and tirzepatide <!-- image --> ## Agents - Exenatide - Liraglutide - Lixisenatide - Semaglutide - Dulaglutide - *Tirzepatide - (GLP-1R and GLP-1R/GIP-R Dual Agonist) <!-- image --> ## GLP-1 Receptor Agonists ## Side Effects: - GI most common (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea), pancreatitis, cholecystitis - medullary thyroid cancer/ C cell hyperplasia in rats, no

## SGLT2 inhibitors

Agents: Canagliflozin, Dapagliflozin, Empagliflozin, Ertugliflozin, Bexagliflozin

MOA: SGLT2 (sodium glucose transporter) responsible in reabsorption of glucose in proximal tubule of the kidney. SGLT2 inhibitors reduce glucose reabsorption, thus increasing glycosuria

Effect on weight: 2- 3Kg reduction

Hba1c: 0.5-1% reduction

## Adverse reactions:

- Hypovolemia, hyperkalemia
- Genital mycotic and urinary tract infections (3 -fold risk)
- Acute kidney injury
- Euglycemia ketoacidosis

## Classification of Hypoglycemia

Level 1: A glucose alert value of 70 mg/dL or less. Level 2: A glucose level of 54 mg/dL is sufficiently low to indicate potentially serious, clinically important hypoglycemia. Level 3: Severe hypoglycemia, as defined by the ADA, denotes severe cognitive impairment requiring external assistance for recovery. Ibrahim M, Baker J, Cahn A, et al. Hypoglycemia and its management in primary care setting [published online ahead of print, 2020 Apr 28]. Diabetes Metab Res Rev.

2020;e3332. doi:10.1002/dmrr.3332 <!-- image --> ## Hypoglycemia and Intervention ## Hypoglycemia - ◦Common complication - ◦Major limiting factors to optimal glycemic control ## Intervention - ◦"rule of 15" - 15 gram of fast-acting carbohydrates (1/2 cup of milk/juice/soda) - Check glucose in 15 minutes, if glucose below 70mg/dl, repeat - If glucose is above 70mg/dl, eat a normal snack or meal <!-- image --> ## Glucagon <!-- image --> Indicated as a treatment for severe hypoglycemia, which may occur in patients with diabetes mellitus.
